extracted.intended_audience: business school students and instructors; readers of corporate ethics case studies
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze a corporate-ethics case study focused on causes, decision‑makers, cultural factors, harms, and recovery strategies following corporate misconduct (Wells Fargo fake-accounts and related scandals). Intended for classroom discussion and ethical evaluation of organizational behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to stakeholders over short-term gains
rubrics_metrics.description: Wells Fargo must put their duty to stakeholders above the company’s aim to make short-term gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking a more long-term, ethical approach would benefit stakeholders and the firm. The case argues that prioritizing short-term revenue and aggressive targets led to illegal customer harm and reputational damage; a long-term duty-focused approach would help rebuild trust over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of practice with stated Vision and Values
rubrics_metrics.description: The illicit activities directly conflicted with Wells Fargo’s publicly expressed Vision and Values, which state the bank strives to set 'the standard among the world’s great companies for integrity and principled performance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether company actions reflect public commitments (e.g., 'We value what’s right for our customers in everything we do'). Misalignment indicates ethical failure and damages credibility; remediation should re-emphasize and operationalize stated values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable and monitored sales goals / incentive structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sales goals were unrealistic and coercive; evidence shows these controversial sales goals most likely encouraged employees to open accounts without customers’ permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria include whether goals are achievable, whether incentive compensation is structured to reward legitimate behavior, and whether systems are in place to ensure employees are actually engaging in legitimate selling. Anti-patterns: aggressive cross-selling quotas with no verification systems; teleological justification ('ends justify means').

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership responsibility and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior management failed to communicate appropriate sales practices and failed to make sure employees were using appropriate practices, indicating ethical indifference at the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether executives set realistic goals, supervised implementation, and intervened when misconduct signs appeared. Examples: executives setting unrealistic targets, alleged awareness of wrongdoing without corrective action, and board failures to ensure effective oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial and branch-level accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers at many branches played a large role in establishing unauthorized accounts and faced termination if branches did not meet goals; managers implemented procedures to ensure goals were met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider local management practices and whether they pressured employees or incentivized shortcuts. Evaluate whether managers were held accountable for fostering ethical practices versus merely meeting targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower protection and response to reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Several employees reported misconduct and claimed termination as a result; whistleblowers allege retaliation, which would violate laws protecting whistleblowers from retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: existence and effectiveness of hotlines, protections against retaliation, and whether reports are investigated and acted upon. Anti-patterns: retaliation, firing reporters, ignoring early warnings (e.g., a 2007 letter describing fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt reporting and remediation of discovered misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting the misconduct early might have actually enhanced Wells Fargo’s reputation as it would have shown the bank had no tolerance for unethical behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate timeliness and transparency of internal and external disclosures, corrective actions taken, refunds to harmed customers, and structural fixes. Examples: refunds to mortgage and auto customers; federal fines; but delayed or insufficient remedial steps worsen reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of customer consent and prevention of fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Wells Fargo issued credit cards without customers’ authorization, misusing assumed consent; customer signatures were often forged, making these activities fraudulent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mechanisms ensuring explicit consent for account openings and product additions, audit trails for authorization, and controls to prevent forgery and assumed consent abuses. Harm metrics include number of unauthorized accounts and customer fee impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and rebuilding of customer trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The banking and financial services industry depends on a public perception of trustworthiness; when a bank puts the company’s interests above depositors, consumer trust shatters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate customer retention/opening trends, public communications (e.g., ad campaigns), restitution efforts, and demonstrable cultural changes. Example metrics: checking account openings fell 43%; credit card applications fell 55% after the scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate culture that is intolerant of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing a strong ethical culture that is intolerant of misconduct will allow Wells Fargo to avoid future scandals and rebuild trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for continuous reinforcement of values, training, incentives aligned with ethical behavior, non-retaliation policies, and leadership modeling. Anti-patterns: cultural acceptance of lying, reward systems that incentivize illegal shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational structure and internal controls to reduce silos and misconduct propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wells Fargo reorganized divisions, reduced management levels, and created a strategic execution and operations unit to focus more on customers and reduce 'silos' that might have contributed to misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether structural changes promote oversight, cross-functional accountability, simplified customer-focused processes, and reduce perverse incentives. Examples: combining banking groups, reducing regions for advisors, creating units to work with regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory compliance and cooperation, and acceptance of regulatory remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators imposed fines and restrictions (e.g., CFPB fines, Federal Reserve growth cap); Wells Fargo must address regulatory issues as part of recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria include cooperation with investigations, acceptance of penalties, remedial plans that meet regulator conditions, and transparency with authorities. Failure to comply leads to penalties, growth restrictions, and ongoing scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive accountability and compensation clawbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives have been asked to 'claw back' money paid during the period the accounts were opened without permission; former CEO Stumpf was forced to pay back millions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether boards hold executives accountable (clawbacks, terminations, reparation), and whether governance changes are made to prevent repeat misconduct. Board oversight failures are highlighted as key contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical reasoning: means matter as much as ends (deontological emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wells Fargo adopted a short-term perspective and abandoned a deontological approach; according to deontology, the means of attaining an outcome are as important morally as the outcome itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether policies and incentives respect ethical process constraints (not just outcomes). Promote ethical frameworks that forbid harmful means even when outcomes (e.g., sales) look positive; use ethical theory to evaluate corporate decisions.
